title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
Udio is an AI music generation system that produces songs with vocals and instruments from text prompts. The central failure here is one of training data provenance: the system was built using copyrighted recordings without the rights holders' authorisation. This is a data-acquisition problem that occurs before deployment, during the construction of the model itself, and it is the kind of problem that licensing due diligence, conducted before training begins, would be designed to catch.

The legal picture is multi-party and unresolved. Universal Music Group settled its claims and entered a licensing arrangement with Udio. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging Udio's models were trained on more than 30,000 recordings, and a judge declined to allow those recordings to be added to an existing case, prompting Sony to file a new action. A copyright class action brought by independent artists was allowed to proceed but transferred to a different court. A musicians' union lawsuit over the UMG deal is also active.

What is not established is whether any court has found Udio liable for copyright infringement; the lawsuits and allegations remain unresolved findings, and settlements reached so far do not constitute admissions of liability.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has settled its lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which was accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The companies have reached licensing agreements, with Udio agreeing to launch a new platform next year that will only use authorized and licensed music. Under the deal, artists can opt in to participate and will receive compensation, though specific financial terms and artist details were not disclosed. UMG's leadership stated the settlement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technology and business models.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, allows users to create original music from text prompts. The company generates songs with voices and instruments but was previously accused of creating content similar to well-known hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission. This marks Udio's first major music licensing agreement with a major label. The company has attracted millions of users since launching and counts music artist will.i.am and venture firm Andreessen Horowitz among its backers.
